subject: research/mimic-whitebox
professional: an adversarial-ML / NLP security researcher who reviews machine-generated-text detection papers (ACL/EMNLP, USENIX Security); first checks: does the table rerun, is there a blind baseline showing white-box knowledge matters, are there intervals, is the attack's edited text natural or does it leave a trivially detectable fingerprint, is the adaptive-defender result confounded by that fingerprint, and is the nearest prior work (Lowd & Meek 2005 good-word attacks on linear spam filters; RAID's own adversarial attacks; DIPPER paraphrase evasion) cited.

evidence.correctness: Reran `cd research/mimic-whitebox && /usr/bin/python3.13 whitebox.py` (1m26s, sklearn 1.9.1): results.txt and results.json byte-identical to the committed files (cmp: identical; git status clean). Independent script /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-oss-monorepo/f091d3e5-eb30-514d-8285-e6f58aa0a1bf/scratchpad/mw/indep.py recomputes AUROC with a Mann-Whitney rank formula (scipy rankdata, not sklearn): k=0 0.947802 (committed 0.947802), delete k=10 0.737659, k=20 0.487135, swap k=10 0.624837, k=20 0.317074 - all match. Filler word recomputed by own argmin loop over the unigram vocabulary: 'is', weight -3.234 - matches. Bootstrap 95% CI (1000 row resamples) for delete k=20: [0.461, 0.512], so the 'chance' reading holds. The numbers are right; their interpretation is where it fails (swap artifact, see domain/claims). No intervals are published at all, so 3 not 4.
evidence.completeness: README promises: the k sweep 0-40 for delete and swap, fixed and adaptive detectors, results.txt/json, figure.svg, 5 tests, ~1.5 min runtime. All present and working: 5 tests pass (`python3.13 -m unittest discover -s tests`, 0.006 s), rerun 1m26s, figure.py draws all four series from results.json (svg in tree matches the committed numbers). Next steps (black-box query budget, zero-shot score run, mimic-loop) are honestly marked as not done. Stated programme scope is a small preliminary slice and it delivers it.
evidence.verification: 5 unit tests, all green. They check k=0 identity, that delete shortens text, swap keeps word count, a 3-word delete lowers the toy score, and that results.json's last delete AUROC is below the first. No test pins any committed number or the adaptive refit. quality_mutate.py, 4 mutants in core logic, 3 survived: ranking reversed so the attack edits the LEAST machine-ward words (whitebox.py:50) - survived; filler picks the most MACHINE-ward word (min->max, whitebox.py:66) - survived; adaptive detector refit on unattacked training text (whitebox.py:85, which silently turns the headline adaptive column into the baseline) - survived; only flipping the contribution sign (whitebox.py:48) was caught. 1 of 4 caught: 1.
evidence.craft: Read whitebox.py (100 lines), figure.py, tests/test_whitebox.py. Compact and readable, reuses mimic-contexts' loader and split unchanged. Defects: dead branch at whitebox.py:56 (`out[-1].isspace() is False and not out[-1].strip()` can only be true for an empty string, so the `continue` never runs; harmless because the token is dropped either way, but it reads as if it handles spacing); files written with bare open() without close (json.dump(..., open(...)) at :91, :97); delete mode collapses every run of 2+ spaces in the whole machine text, not only at edit sites (:61), a side edit on the attacked class only; the attack ranks by unigram contribution but deletion also removes all bigrams containing the word, not modelled. README repeats the 'Live page' line twice (README.md:3 and :7).
evidence.claims: Backed: baseline 0.948 vs 0.927 for the full detector (mimic-contexts results), every number in the Result paragraph (rerun), 'held-out poetry, reviews and wiki only', 900 of 1800 machine, filler 'is', 'preliminary, stylised, one seed, no fluency check' disclaimers, AI-assistance and no-affiliation notes. Not backed or misleading: (1) 'Swapping those words for one human-ward filler word is faster' - my one-feature probe (share of tokens equal to 'is') separates swapped machine text from human text at AUROC 0.9991 (k=10) and 0.99999 (k=20), against 0.516 unattacked: the swap attack evades this detector only by writing text any counter flags, and the adaptive 1.000 for swap is the refit learning that one feature, not evidence of a robust defender. (2) '~10-20 edited word types per text' - at k=20 delete removes a median 14.8% of each machine text's word tokens (8.5% at k=10); the budget in tokens is not reported. (3) 'A defender who refits ... wins it all back and more' is stated without the confound above and without intervals. Live page returned 000 through this container's proxy (not verified).
evidence.fitness: A researcher can rerun and extend it in two minutes; the split and detector are shared with mimic-contexts/evade, so results are comparable within the track. But: no blind baseline is reported. I ran one (indep.py, random_attack: delete/swap k random in-vocabulary word types, seed 1): delete k=20 random gives 0.945 vs 0.487 white-box, swap k=20 random 0.864 vs 0.317 - so white-box knowledge genuinely matters, which strengthens the paper's point but is not in it. Nearest prior work not cited: Lowd & Meek (2005, CEAS) 'Good word attacks on statistical spam filters' is exactly this attack (add human-ward / remove machine-ward words against a known linear text classifier) and its adaptive-retraining finding; RAID (cited only as text source) itself benchmarks 11 adversarial attacks including synonym swap against detectors; Krishna et al. (2023) DIPPER and Sadasivan et al. (2023) on paraphrase evasion; Shi et al. (2024, TACL) word-substitution red-teaming of detectors. Li et al. 2019 TextBugger is cited, but it targets neural classifiers. The result is a reproduction of a known effect on a new suite, not new: fitness 2.
evidence.domain: Against standard practice for evasion studies (e.g. RAID, DIPPER, adversarial-NLP evaluation norms): requires a blind baseline (absent), intervals over rows/seeds (absent, unlike sibling mimic-evade which reports paired bootstrap CIs), an edit-budget measured in tokens or edit distance, and a naturalness constraint or at least a fingerprint check on attacked text (absent; the swap fingerprint is near-perfectly detectable). The adaptive-defender column trains on attacked machine text with untouched humans, so it conflates 'robust detector' with 'detector of this attack's artifact'; the README's Limitations notes the single-attack caveat but not the artifact. Greedy unigram ranking with no query limit is a reasonable white-box upper-bound proxy and is honestly described. Departures make it short of a reviewer's sign-off: 2.

defects.what: The swap result and its adaptive column are driven by a trivial fingerprint: every edited word becomes 'is', so the share of 'is' tokens alone separates swapped machine text from human text at AUROC 0.9991 (k=10). The README presents swap as the 'faster' evasion and the adaptive 1.000 as the defender winning, without saying either is an artifact of the filler.
No blind baseline: the paper never shows that knowing the weights matters. A random-k edit (my run) leaves AUROC at 0.945 (delete k=20) vs 0.487 white-box; this should be a column.

Nearest prior work not cited: Lowd & Meek (2005) good-word attacks on linear spam filters (same attack and same retraining defence), RAID's own adversarial-attack benchmark, DIPPER (Krishna et al. 2023), Shi et al. (2024) substitution red-teaming. Only TextBugger is cited.
No intervals on any AUROC or adaptive gap (sibling mimic-evade reports paired bootstrap CIs); edit budget reported in word types only, hiding that k=20 deletes a median 14.8% of tokens.
3 of 4 seeded mutants survive, including the adaptive refit silently using unattacked text and the attack ranking reversed; test_committed_results checks only that the last AUROC is below the first.
Dead branch: `elif out and out[-1].isspace() is False and not out[-1].strip()` is true only for an empty string, so the `continue` never runs.
'Live page' line duplicated at README.md:3 and :7.

verdict: A small, honest, preliminary slice that reproduces exactly: rerunning whitebox.py gives byte-identical results, and an independent Mann-Whitney AUROC and argmin-filler check match every number (0.948 baseline; delete k=20 0.487, bootstrap CI 0.461-0.512). The numbers are right; the research design is not at a reviewer's bar. The swap attack, sold as the faster evasion, replaces words with 'is' so that a one-feature 'is' counter separates attacked machine text from human text at AUROC 0.999, which also explains the swap adaptive 1.000. There is no blind baseline (a random-k edit leaves AUROC at 0.945, so white-box knowledge does matter, but the project never shows it), no intervals, the budget hides that k=20 deletes ~15% of tokens, and the nearest prior work (Lowd & Meek's good-word attacks, RAID's attack suite, DIPPER) is uncited, so the novelty is a known effect on a new suite. 3 of 4 seeded mutants survive. Does not meet the bar.
